description: Somos unas personas interesadas en la tecnología, la inteligencia artificial y la innovación con impacto social. Desarrollo ROTA-AGRO , un proyecto que combina datos de la NASA e IA para ayudar a agricultores a tomar mejores decisiones y enfrentar riesgos climáticos.
summary:
What happens when drought, pests and falling prices hit one after another? Today, farmers find out alone, when it's already too late.
We designed ROTA-AGRO, a tool that tells farmers which crop rotation can survive that chain of shocks. It combines NASA data (Landsat, HLS, SMAP, NASA POWER) with soil conditions in each micro-zone, phone photos, low-cost sensors and what the family knows about the land. It generates several five-year rotations and stress-tests them in a compound stress simulator built on Monte Carlo, measuring the probability of failing to cover costs and household food. It speaks by voice, works offline and reaches farmers through messaging.
What sets us apart: we treat ancestral knowledge as a hypothesis validated against satellite data, not passive input, and we turn crop residue into income through mushrooms, briquettes and compost.
It matters because the climate is shifting, water is getting scarce and soils are wearing out, while farmers decide with scattered data and no fair credit. ROTA-AGRO turns NASA's view from space into evidence a farmer can understand, and links the decision to income, credit, insurance and markets.
The farmer decides. We give them the tools.
details:
Every season, a farmer has to decide what to plant without knowing whether the rain will come, whether a pest will move in, or what the harvest will fetch at market. The hard part is that these things rarely happen one at a time. A drought weakens the soil, weak soil invites pests, and then prices fall. Most farmers face that chain alone, with scattered data, no fair credit, and nobody giving weight to what their family has learned over generations.

ROTA-AGRO is a decision-support tool that helps farmers pick crop rotations that can hold up under pressure. We pair NASA Earth observations with everything else that shapes a farmer's choice: soil, water, money, market, community and inherited knowledge. It's meant for small and semi-commercial farmers, owners or tenants, along with their families, with technicians and cooperatives alongside them. The project started in the Colombian countryside, on a database from Boyacá, Antioquia and Valle del Cauca, and we want it to reach other countries.

Why now? The climate is shifting, water is getting scarce and soils are wearing down, so every planting decision carries more risk. Existing tools compare rotations against soil and climate data and stop there. We think the missing piece is everything around that data, and ROTA-AGRO puts it into one flow.

In practice, it starts with the plot itself. It reads NASA satellite data (Landsat and HLS for vegetation and its history, SMAP for soil moisture, NASA POWER for weather), adds Sentinel-2 imagery, cheap local sensors and photos taken with the farmer's phone, and splits the field into micro-zones. From that it estimates soil condition without an expensive lab test, and it says plainly how uncertain those estimates are. When something is missing, like crop history or water sources, the AI asks the farmer rather than guessing. It also learns from each season.

Then it generates several possible rotations, projects them five years out as scenarios, and compares them on resilience, income, food for the household, soil and water, without hiding the trade-offs inside a single score. Rotations that don't fit the farmer's equipment, labor, seeds or land lease get dropped. The answer comes in the farmer's own words, through a light app with voice, short messages, traffic-light icons and offline mode, or through a messaging bot where there's no signal. Each recommendation shows where its data came from and how sure we are.

In our example conversation, the bot tells the owner of "Lote Las Margaritas" that moisture has dropped and only the north zone needs water, that the bean harvest is twelve days away, and asks whether the leftover stalks should become mushroom beds or compost.

The piece we're proudest of is the compound stress simulator. Instead of asking how a rotation does in an average year, it tests what happens when things go wrong in sequence, and it estimates the probability that the farmer can't cover production costs or feed the household. We start with four chains: drought, then pests, then a price drop; heat and drought, then lower yields and costlier inputs; too much rain, then disease and post-harvest losses; and a late frost, then replanting and a forced sale at a low price. The assumptions are editable, and Monte Carlo simulation varies how severe each shock is and in what order they hit.

Three more things set us apart. We treat ancestral knowledge as a hypothesis worth testing. A family's practice gets written down in their own words, checked against satellite records, and reported as confirmed, inconclusive or contradicted. If it's contradicted, we don't call it a mistake, because what a farmer sees on one plot and what a satellite sees across a region can both be true. Crop residue, which is usually burned or lost, becomes mushrooms, crafts, briquettes and compost. And the farm decision connects to credit, insurance and markets. We also publish how accurate we've been, instead of promising certainty.

We're building this in phases, each one resting on the last. Phase one is the decision core: soil diagnosis, rotation comparison, the stress simulator and a voice interface. Phase two tests it with five to ten farmers or technicians. Phase three adds cost tracking by voice, residue use and short training capsules. Phase four brings credit, insurance, markets and coordination between neighbors who share a watershed. Phase five is expansion, one region at a time, and only after recalibrating with local data.

The tools we plan to use are NASA data (Landsat, HLS, SMAP, NASA POWER and NISAR) and Sentinel-2 through Google Earth Engine; NOAA and European Centre weather data; FAO soil maps and SoilGrids; Monte Carlo simulation and backtesting; speech recognition; a mobile app and messaging bot; and basic soil moisture meters and rain gauges.

For a farmer, this could mean choosing with evidence, knowing whether a rotation leaves enough to live and eat on during the transition, earning something from crop residue, and seeing what each kilo really costs by logging expenses out loud. The record it builds can help open doors to credit, insurance and markets, and the three-minute lessons download in town and play without using data.

For the community, neighbors who draw on the same aquifer can coordinate, share freight and negotiate together, and soils get healthier. The project contributes to ten Sustainable Development Goals, including no poverty, zero hunger, clean water and climate action. Those are expected contributions that we'll measure in the pilot.

Some things shaped every decision. The farmer decides, and the data is theirs, under the CARE principles. Nobody should be shut out for lacking signal, reading skills or a financial history, which is why voice and offline mode come first. And we're upfront about the limits: Andean cloud cover, satellites that can't measure nutrients directly, financial regulation, the risk of bias in credit scoring, and the need to recalibrate before moving to a new place.

Where we stand: ROTA-AGRO is a complete design, built in phases. Anything that needs local data gets calibrated and validated in the pilot with technicians and farmers. We'll backtest against a past event such as El Niño 2015-16 and measure error, calibration, whether farmers change their decisions, and whether they understand the recommendation. The numerical targets are goals to measure, not results.

NASA gives us the view from above. Our job is to turn it into a decision a farmer can trust, carry out and keep up for years, and to show with evidence how far that trust should go.
